figures.description: Service Limit State for Lateral Displacements Lateral displacement check for bridge foundations, retaining walls, and noise/sign structures at service loads φ = 1.0 for Service Limit State — no resistance reduction factor applied Tolerable lateral displacement is set by structural engineer, not geotechnical engineer p-y analysis is the recommended method for Service Limit State displacement analysis Displacement limits are often governed by structural performance (joint closure, excessive lean) Steel piles can typically sustain more displacement than structures can tolerate

figures.caption: Design procedure for laterally loaded deep foundations (continued next page)
figures.description: Design Process All projects requiring laterally loaded deep foundation design Block 1: Establish project type, performance requirements, load factors, and tolerable deflection criteria Block 9 contains four sub-analyses: geotechnical strength LS, structural strength LS, service LS, extreme event LS Blocks 9 and 11 (single pile and group analysis) are the primary analytical activities of lateral design Block 13 constructability review is important for foundation type selection and specification development Process is iterative — multiple loops between blocks are common in practice

figures.description: Broms Method Preliminary analysis, simple structures (sign posts, noise walls, light poles) in uniform profiles; Strength Limit State only Applicable only to short, stiff piles that rotate (not bend) with free-head rotation Cohesive soil: max resistance = 9Su × B (top 1.5B ignored); key depth parameter f = Pt/(9SuB) Cohesionless soil: max resistance = 3Bγz Kp; depth to max moment f = √[Pt/(1.5BγKp)] Not calibrated to LRFD; use with engineering judgment for simple structures Broms long pile deflection method is NOT recommended — use p-y analysis instead

figures.description: Other Design Considerations All single pile p-y analyses where scour, sloping ground, axial loads, or fixity conditions are relevant design parameters Depth of fixity (clay): df = 1.4 × (EpIw/Es)^0.25 (Eq. 6-18); verify by p-y analysis in final design Depth of fixity (sand): df = 1.8 × (EpIw/nh)^0.2 (Eq. 6-19) Fixed head piles carry higher head moment; free head piles have larger deflection Scour: remove lateral soil resistance over scoured depth in p-y analysis Include axial load Px in p-y analysis — it increases bending moments via P-delta effects

figures.description: Group Effects in Lateral Loading: Group Efficiency and P-Multipliers Groups of closely spaced deep foundations where pile-soil-pile interaction reduces lateral resistance; p-y method group analysis Group efficiency Ge = Qg/(n*Qs); Ge ≤ 1.0 for closely spaced groups P-multiplier Pm reduces p-y curves by row: leading row highest Pm, trailing rows progressively lower Table 7-1: at 3B spacing, Pm = 0.8/0.4/0.3 (Rows 1/2/3+); at 5B, Pm = 1.0/0.85/0.7 Group spacing, size, and layout dominate Pm; soil type and density have secondary influence Pm values are essentially constant for pile head deflections above about 3/4 inch P-multipliers apply only to p-y method; Broms method is single-pile only

figures.caption: Example plots of load versus pile head deflection pile and bending moment versus pile head deflection for pile group analysis using single pile p-y analysis (modified from Hannigan et al. 2006, originally adapted from Brown and Bollman 1993)
figures.description: Analysis of Groups of Deep Foundation Elements Groups of deep foundations under lateral loading — from preliminary analysis to complex nonlinear group software Individual pile analysis with Pm per row is acceptable for preliminary/non-critical structures Weighted average Pm approach (Brown et al. 2010): apply overstress factor 1.2/1.15/1.05 at 3B/4B/5B Nonlinear group software preferred for critical structures — captures cap rotation, pile cap effects Default software p-multipliers may over-predict group resistance by ~35% (Rollins et al. 2000) FEM can model group as continuum but generally not cost-effective for routine design Group software may not address settlement, downdrag, and elastic shortening — check separately

figures.caption: Variation of foundation response for vertical and batter piles (modified from Wilson et al. 2006)
figures.description: Use of Batter Piles Foundation groups incorporating batter piles for lateral load resistance; should be avoided in seismic areas and where significant settlement is expected Batter piles resist lateral loads through horizontal component of axial force; typical batter 1H:12V to 1H:3V Batter piles generally discouraged in seismic areas — higher stiffness amplifies demand, poor ductility in compression Settlement and downdrag cause additional bending moments in batter piles; downdrag must be included in design Design sequence: design vertical piles first; add batter piles only if vertical piles are insufficient P-y analysis uses modifying constant (0–2) for pult: 0–1 for pile inclined toward load, 1–2 away from load

figures.description: Structural Design of Steel Foundation Elements Structural design of steel H-pile and pipe pile foundation elements under combined axial, bending, and shear loading Steel axial compression: 3-step — yield resistance P0, buckling Pe (flexural or torsional), nominal Pn Pn = P0×0.658^(P0/Pe) when Pe/P0 ≥ 0.44; Pn = 0.877×Pe when Pe/P0 < 0.44 H-pile flexure: compact section (λf ≤ λpf) → Mn = 1.5×Fy×Sy; noncompact → interpolated (Eq 11-42) Pipe pile flexure: compact (D/t ≤ 0.07E/Fy) → Mn = Fy×Zy; local buckling governs at higher D/t Combined axial-bending: biaxial interaction checks (Eq 11-47/11-48) — applies to vertical piles only Torsional buckling check required for H-piles extending through air or water (open section, doubly symmetric)

figures.caption: Example of a two-way lateral load test set-up for a drilled shaft
figures.description: Test Methods Lateral load test methods for driven piles and drilled shafts — static, rapid, and bi-directional ASTM D3966 Procedures A–H: defines static test variations — monotonic, cyclic, sustained, reversed, and combined loading Typical setup: hydraulic jack against reaction pile, deadweight, or anchor system; load cell and LVDTs/dial gauges measure load and deflection Free-head test (no head moment) is most common; fixed-head requires a rigid connection frame Rapid load test (Statnamic): dynamic force of short duration; requires inertia/damping correction for equivalent static response Bi-directional test: embedded hydraulic jack self-reacts; eliminates surface reaction system but requires full internal instrumentation

figures.caption: Example of a one-way lateral load test set up on a deep foundation
figures.description: Instrumentation Instrumentation planning for laterally loaded deep foundation tests — external and internal monitoring External: LVDTs/dial gauges for head deflection (multiple elevations), load cells for applied force, tiltmeters for head rotation VW strain gauge pairs (diametrically opposed) at ~1–3D intervals: curvature φ from differential bending strain Bending moment from curvature: M = E×I×φ (Eq 12-2); E×I must account for temporary casing if left in place Inclinometer casings: deflection profile from integrated inclination readings; requires separate probe insertion after each step Shape Acceleration Arrays (SAAs): MEMS-based continuous real-time deflection profiling without probe insertion

figures.description: Data Analysis Analysis of internal instrumentation data from lateral load tests to derive deflection, bending moment, and p-y curves Deflection profile: y = ∫∫φ dz² (double integration of curvature, Eq 12-1); constants from head boundary conditions Bending moment: M = E×I×φ (Eq 12-2); composite EI must account for reinforcing cage and any permanent casing Soil resistance: p = −d²M/dz² (Eq 12-3); direct numerical differentiation of sparse discrete data is impractical Piecewise polynomial (Dunnavant 1986): 5th-order polynomial fit to five-point windows (Eq 12-4), double-differentiated analytically Minimum five strain gauge pairs required for piecewise polynomial approach; more pairs improves p-y accuracy Zero-moment at load application point (or known ground-line moment) should be imposed
